Non-binary recognition is absent and healthcare capacity is tiny, so gender-affirming care requires travel.

Visitor-facing evidence is unusually direct: verified 2026 destination guides describe a discreet luxury culture — full legal protections, 'a cosmopolitan crowd that genuinely doesn't care', no organised scene but complete safety for same-sex couples — and the rights overview reports the collectivity attracts trans residents from less accepting neighbours. A current-status review tempers that surface: local acceptance runs lower than the visitor economy implies, though no legal regression exists. Read: protected and comfortable, shallow community depth, care requires travel.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Adjacent assessment context: a rights-rating page scores this collectivity among the strongest frameworks in the region, and the current-status review that confirms no regression dates from 2026 — both weight the thin local record toward the parent nation's practice rather than local enforcement.

rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Collectivity of France; local deviations noted in the summary. The framework-wide prison findings concern detention conditions and are unresolved for visitor-facing practice; whether local acceptance figures track the visitor-economy picture is not independently measured.

rewrites.summary:
An autonomous constituent country within a Western European kingdom, Aruba legislates positively rather than merely tolerating: its parliament voted 11-5 in 2016 to open registered unions carrying married-couple benefits (pension succession, emergency medical decisions), and the official tourism authority runs a dedicated LGBT programme marketing the destination as welcoming to all visitors, with nearly a hundred nationalities resident.

Travel-culture reporting through the kingdom's networks characterises Aruba, with its two sister islands, as quiet, tolerant and mostly open — a small, stable, tourism-dependent society. The parliamentary vote's own record notes religious and cultural opposition to full equal marriage, which remains unlegislated, and no local gender-recognition or specialist-care pathway is evidenced. No enforcement against trans or same-sex visitors is documented anywhere in the record: protection by registered partnership and tourism economics rather than full equality.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: By the government's own account, the 2016 vote made Aruba the first in the region to act on registered unions. Religious and cultural opposition, recorded in the very account of the parliamentary vote, confined the outcome to partnerships rather than full equal marriage — a regional-comparison context rather than anything enforceable against visitors.
rewrites.localsOnly: No purely resident-facing datum is documented for Aruba beyond the general record: no local discrimination survey or resident testimony appears in the dossier, and the registered-union framework governs residents as it governs visitors.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands; local deviations noted in the summary. Whether the registered-union pathway is ever exercised by visitors, and whether the absence of documented enforcement reflects absence or non-reporting, is unresolved: the record rests on official tourism self-description and kingdom-network travel reporting, with no independent local enforcement data.

rewrites.summary: An autonomous constituent country of the same kingdom, Curaçao's audited record is one of official intent colliding with friction. For a visitor the composite reads as low legal risk with thin infrastructure: no documented state hostility, an active but negotiating community in the capital, and no evidenced local gender-recognition pathway or care capacity. Travel-culture surveys place the destination inside the region's quiet tolerant mainstream.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Local institutions are contested rather than hostile: in 2015 representatives of all the parent nation's governments agreed on an equal-rights package for regional LGBT residents, yet the same reporting documents Pride permit difficulties as recently as 2013 and organised parliamentary opposition that the destination's own government publicly opposed while supporting the community.
rewrites.localsOnly: No resident-facing fact specific to Curaçao is documented in the dossier beyond the community-organising record; the equal-rights package and permitting practice govern residents as they govern visitors, with no resident discrimination data recorded.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands; local deviations noted in the summary. rewrites.summary:
These are not autonomous countries but special municipalities of the kingdom itself, so metropolitan equality law applies directly: same-sex marriage has been performed on the islands since 2012 — one small island hosted the region's first such wedding after the 2010 status change and markets civil ceremonies openly — with the state's penal-code discrimination grounds and partnership frameworks in force, and a current-status review confirming no later change.

The caveats are real: legal gender change still requires a medical expert's statement (the self-declaration act was withdrawn at kingdom level in July 2025), non-binary markers demand months-long court procedure, and three tiny church-dense communities leave service depth thin — the same rights overview that documents these gaps rates them with the metropolitan standard attached. Travel-side evidence is warm and wedding-positive; no adverse enforcement is documented.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Assessment context: a current-status review confirms no later change to the applied position, and the rights overview rates the destination with the metropolitan standard attached. The self-declaration act's withdrawal at kingdom level (July 2025) is a parent-state statutory shift, not a local decision — regional-comparison context rather than local statutes.
rewrites.localsOnly: Three tiny church-dense communities limit service depth for residents as for visitors, and no resident-specific discrimination data or local surveys appear in the dossier.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Special municipalities of the Kingdom of the Netherlands; local deviations noted in the summary. The dossier records same-sex marriage performed since 2012 while the freshness confirmation cites 2018 — the earliest-performed date is unresolved; how the medical-expert gender-change statement is applied in practice is unverified.

rewrites.summary:
A self-governing part of the Realm of Denmark: domestic equality and family law are set locally, beneath a national human-rights framework. Same-sex marriage arrived only in 2017, late for the Nordics, after church-state friction. Nothing in the audited record criminalises trans people or documents enforcement against them.

The climate is measured by politics rather than prosecution: for a visitor that reads as low violence risk, thin legal protection, and high-profile political hostility to visibility.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Political climate as recorded: in 2010 a local legislator refused to share a state banquet with another country's gay premier, calling the pairing 'a direct provocation', and was still demanding Pride bans in 2015, when a nationally beloved singer urged the public to ignore him.
rewrites.localsOnly: In 2006 activists gathered some 20,000 signatures — a large share of a ~50,000 population — demanding anti-discrimination protection after surveys found violence and discrimination against out gay residents 'not uncommon' and legally unaddressed.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Self-governing part of the Kingdom of Denmark; local deviations noted in the summary. The record's reporting is dated (2006-2015); no later evidence confirms whether the political hostility persists, and the petition figure is described as 'some', not exact.

rewrites.summary:
A self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark, with its own parliament and courts for domestic law. For a visitor the picture is low-friction: gay life is described as 'almost a non-event' — integrated, non-violent, modest, with a small Pride since 2010. Marriage equality was adopted from Danish legislation in 2016, passed unanimously by the local parliament with the established church's bishop supportive; in the same year the state/province took a self-declaration approach to gender recognition, ahead of the parent state's own practice.

The counterweight is capacity, not hostility: a population spread across remote settlements means thin institutional reach and limited services, and anonymity comes from isolation rather than crowds.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Institutional history: the 1996 partnership law came from the Danish model with virtually no debate, and the 2016 marriage provisions were adopted from Danish legislation rather than drafted locally — context that frames local statute as import rather than innovation.
rewrites.localsOnly: The local equality society (named Qaamaneq, founded 2014) serves lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender residents — the resident-facing organisational record in the dossier; no other local discrimination data appears.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Self-governing territory of the Kingdom of Denmark; local deviations noted in the summary. The dossier's reporting dates to 2014-2016; whether the self-declaration practice and service levels persist is not confirmed by later evidence, and the population figure derives from the travel reporting rather than official statistics.

rewrites.summary:
A US territory where the federal anti-trans turn of 2025-26 — document/marker rules and screening friction — applies in full. In July 2025 the governor signed the most severe ban on gender-affirming care in the country, criminalising provision of hormones or surgery to anyone under 21 even with parental consent: up to 15 years' imprisonment, $50,000 fines, and loss of medical licences, with parents potentially exposed. Civil-rights groups announced court challenges.

For a trans visitor today: national paperwork friction, the harshest local care-crime regime in the country, and a visible advocacy community pushing back in court.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The parent nation's turbulence and local politics frame the destination from outside its own statutes: the same 2025-26 turn carries a military-service exclusion, and the care ban is benchmarked as the most severe in the country — comparative context; the signatory had campaigned presenting as LGBTQ-friendly. Local politics have swung both ways: the island's marriage ban was dismantled in the national courts after local couples sued (2014), and religious-freedom and conversion-therapy bills advanced in 2019 before the governor withdrew them under organised pressure.
rewrites.localsOnly: Residents face the care ban's implementation design: the law mandates department campaigns warning against affirming care, passed through non-public hearings, and is drafted vaguely so that doctors and parents facilitating hormones or surgery risk prosecution — the record's only resident-specific material.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Unincorporated US territory; local deviations noted in the summary. Court challenges to the care ban were announced but their outcomes are unresolved, and how the deliberately vague provisions will be enforced in practice is unverified; the 2014 marriage ruling and the 2019 bill episodes are history, not current law.

Applies at the state/province's airports as the national screening procedure — the framework a trans visitor actually stands under.

Washington Blade (26 Apr 2019): the governor announced a religious-freedom bill and a conversion-therapy ban with a pastoral exemption; local advocates said the pairing would open discrimination doors, criticising the religious-freedom carve-out as licence to refuse service on orientation or gender-identity grounds.

Washington Blade (25 Jun 2014): four same-sex couples joined the national marriage lawsuit in the state/province (filed in March), with a national legal organisation and a local advocates' group intervening — one couple married abroad in 2007, another in a different part of the parent nation in 2012; a former national guard member among the plaintiffs. The road to marriage equality in the state/province ran through the national court system.

Washington Blade (18 Mar 2019): the pro-statehood caucus in the local legislature blocked a floor vote on a bill that would have banned conversion therapy for minors; a co-sponsoring legislator dissented publicly. The conversion-therapy ban died in the legislature despite upper-house passage and governor support.

Washington Blade (13 Jun 2019): the governor asked lawmakers to withdraw the religious-freedom and conversion-therapy bill pairing amid sustained opposition; the earlier announcement had included a pastoral-capacity exemption for clergy. A record of local advocates defeating the religious-freedom bill pairing.

Erin in the Morning (2025): the state/province enacted a trans youth care ban pushed through non-public hearings; the law is deliberately vague so that doctors and affirming parents facilitating hormones or surgery risk prosecution; it mandates department campaigns on the 'risks' of affirming care; the enacted text is the most extreme care restriction in the nation, per the report.

rewrites.summary:
An unincorporated US territory carrying a large permanent US military presence, so the 2025-26 federal turn — marker/document policy, screening friction, and the trans military-exclusion order — lands hard here. Local law partly cuts the other way: Guam was the first US territory to recognise same-sex marriage (2015, after a local lesbian couple sued over a denied licence), its statute book bars employment discrimination including gender identity, and federal hate-crime coverage has applied since 2009.

The synthesis for a visitor: real written protections and a quiet, integrated public record, against military-community conservatism, parent-state volatility amplified by the base, and small-community visibility where an outed stranger is noticed.

rewrites.localsOnly: Academic identity surveys record indigenous Chamorro understandings of gender diversity, and a local advocacy scene maintains ID-documents guidance for residents — the record's resident-facing material; no resident discrimination data appears.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Unincorporated US territory; local deviations noted in the summary. Two of the dossier's sources are thin, so the resident record rests on limited material; how the trans military-exclusion order and screening changes are applied to visitors in practice is unverified.
